sec.title: Background
sec.p: The discovery of meningeal lymphatic vessels (mLVs) has reshaped our understanding of brain waste clearance, positioning them as a very important clearance route. However, quantifying the precise hydrodynamics and solute transport mechanisms within the human dura mater in vivo remains highly challenging due to the multiscale nature of cranial fluid dynamics and imaging resolution limits.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We integrated patient-specific intrathecal contrast-enhanced MRI (gMRI) data from a single healthy subject with a novel anatomical segmentation of the cranial dura mater. By employing a hierarchy of inverse mathematical and micro-mechanical models, we estimated previously inaccessible physiological transport parameters. To ensure parameter identifiability, we deliberately modeled a scenario where the meningeal lymphatic vessels act as the sole fluid efflux route, thereby establishing an upper limit for their clearance capacity. These baseline estimates subsequently informed a spatially distributed, double-porosity 3D computational model of the human dura to simulate the fluid dynamics of cranial clearance.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Our analysis suggests that purely diffusive macroscopic models fail to replicate in vivo tracer distribution. Conversely, a dual-porosity advection-diffusion framework successfully captures the tissue kinetics. The transport within the mLV compartment is characterized by highly convective clearance (with Pe > 1), with macroscopic fluid velocities and effective lymphatic diffusion coefficients yielding an upper-bound advective capacity theoretically sufficient to clear the total albumin content in the Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Based on our findings on a single subject (Gonzo) solute clearance within the human cranial dura mater emerges as multiphasic, advection-dominated process. Rather than relying on passive Fickian diffusion, molecules appear to be actively and rapidly cleared through the meningeal lymphatic network via convective mechanisms. While our assumption of exclusively mLV-driven clearance provides a theoretical upper limit for their capacity, this hierarchical modeling approach successfully bridges clinical imaging and microscopic fluid dynamics, offering quantitative insights into the primary mechanical drivers of dural fluid clearance.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The discovery of functional meningeal lymphatic vessels (mLVs) has fundamentally reshaped our understanding of central nervous system (CNS) immune privilege and, crucially, of the fluid dynamic mechanisms governing brain waste clearance [1]. While initially characterized along the dorsal dural sinuses, recent evidence has significantly expanded this anatomical map to include basal and vertebral regions, suggesting a comprehensive and global drainage network [2]. Using computational modeling, we provide the first in vivo estimates of transport properties in dural lymphatics based on a single healthy human subject.

This modern paradigm shift marks the culmination of a scientific narrative that began in 1787 with Paolo Mascagni and 1786 with William Cruikshank, who first described “absorbent vessels” within the human dura [3, 4]. However, Mascagni’s insights were largely suppressed for 150 years by the “venous-only” model proposed by Key and Retzius in 1875, which established arachnoid granulations as the sole exit for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) [5]. The mid-twentieth century work of Lecco and the functional experiments of Földi provided the necessary link between cervical lymphatics and cerebral homeostasis, eventually leading to the definitive molecular characterization of mLVs using markers such as LYVE1 and PROX1 [1, 6–8].

Physiologically, the mLVs act as the essential “downstream” clearance route for the glymphatic system, bridging the gap between the brain parenchyma, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the systemic circulation. In this glial-dependent waste clearance pathway, CSF is propelled through periarterial spaces, mixes with interstitial fluid (ISF), and facilitates the removal of neurotoxic proteins like amyloid-beta (Aβ), tau and alpha-synuclein via perivenous exit routes [9, 10]. Impairments in this glymphatic-lymphatic coupling are increasingly recognized as potential contributing factors to neurodegenerative aging, directly contributing to the proteinopathy observed in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases [10–12].

From a hydraulic perspective, mLVs act as critical efflux pathways, serving as primary drivers for the removal of CSF and metabolic solutes. Consequently, they are thought to play a critical role in maintaining intracranial fluid balance and in influencing the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative diseases [13–15]. However, quantifying the precise hydrodynamics of this system remains challenging due to the multiscale nature of the problem.

In vivo imaging often lacks the resolution to directly measure local flow parameters, such as dural permeability or specific lymphatic clearance rates. Intrathecal contrast enhanced longitudinal MRI (gMRI) is a method for estimating transport properties of solutes in the human brain by studying the evolution of the intrathecal fluid-borne contrast agent gadobutrol, referred to as a tracer [16, 17]. In gMRI, a reference MRI is performed prior to injection of the tracer, and then subsequent MRIs are performed at several time-points following tracer injection. Using the pre-injection reference images we may therefore estimate the concentration of the tracer at each time-point, providing an avenue for exploring solute transport properties in the brain. We employ data from an openly available dataset of one healthy volunteer who underwent gMRI, nicknamed Gonzo [18], with MRI contrast measurements 4, 24, 48 and 72 hours following injection.

To quantify flow parameters of the dura and dural lymphatic vessels, we introduce a new anatomically informed segmentation of the dura, building on previous segmentations of the CSF and parenchyma [19, 20]. We limit the segmentation to the layer of dura lining the skull, which we call the cranial dura. Using this novel segmentation, we estimate average tracer concentrations within the dura and the CSF in the Gonzo dataset. From these estimated values, we solve inverse problems via a hierarchy of reduced-order models and micro-mechanical analyses. This approach allows us to estimate physiological parameter ranges currently inaccessible in vivo, which are subsequently used to parametrize and solve a spatially distributed, 3D numerical simulation of the human dura based on a double-porosity macroscopic model [21–23]. In doing so, this work provides the first assessment of dural lymphatic clearance in a single healthy volunteer by integrating gMRI data with advanced computational modeling, offering a new framework to evaluate the role of the meningeal lymphatics in brain waste-clearance.

Segmentations and parameters derived in this work can be reproduced in their entirety using the code provided in https://github.com/Erasdna/Parameter-estimation-in-the-dura. Detailed installation instructions can be found using this link. Data associated with the project is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21393950.

sec.title: The Gonzo dataset
sec.p: We use The Gonzo MRI Dataset [24], an openly available gMRI dataset from one healthy male subject, nicknamed Gonzo. Gonzo was administered an intrathecal contrast agent (0.25 mmol of gadobutrol, 1 mL) by an interventional radiologist. He then underwent MRI at 3T prior to injection, as well as approximately 4, 24, 48 and 72 hours following injection, allowing us to track the evolution of the tracer in the brain. For a complete overview of the data acquisition involved in the study and all imaging modalities available in the dataset, we refer the reader to Riseth et al. [18].

sec.title: Segmenting the cranial dura
sec.p: In this work, we aim to use gadobutrol concentration values in the cranial dura to estimate transport properties of dural lymphatics and mLVs. Current state-of-the-art brain segmentation tools typically exclude the dura because its thinness (typically 1-2 mm) often prevents it from being fully resolved without sufficient MRI resolution. To address this, we introduce a new anatomy-based method for estimating tracer signal in the cranial dura. In the Gonzo dataset the resolution is mm, making the dura visible in -weighted MRI, but often not clearly distinguishable based only on signal intensity. Particularly the dura between the hemispheres (falx) and between the cerebrum and cerebellum (tentorium cerebelli) can be hard to identify, and we estimate that tracer signal in these regions would be hard to distinguish from CSF at the current resolution. We therefore include only the cranial dura, which lines the skull on the outside of the CSF. This layer of dura only has CSF signal on one side and is therefore easier to separate from pure fluid-based signal.

Accordingly, the first objective when determining tracer signal in the cranial dura is to exclude CSF-based signal to the greatest extent possible. The CSF is identified using the method outlined in [19] by thresholding the SE-image acquired from the Mixed sequence in the pre-contrast MRI session. The CSF can then be segmented by extrapolating parenchymal labels identified using FreeSurfer [20, 27–29]. We create an initial guess for the cranial dura by making a 3-voxel layer outside of the combined parenchyma and CSF segmentation. Subsequently, we use the Look-Locker pre-injection sequence inside this thin ribbon to threshold regions which are most likely to be dura. We set the lower-threshold on the -time in this ribbon to be 400 ms, aiming to remove potential signal-pollution due to fatty tissue [30]. In addition, we set the upper threshold to be the 5th percentile -time of the Look-Locker signal in the CSF mask, which is found to be 1705 ms in this particular subject. We note that this upper bound is considerably lower than the signal range typically used for CSF. We emphasize that this upper bound is an empirical estimate, this threshold is not the only viable choice. However, in this work, we primarily aim to exclude CSF signal to the extent possible while retaining the dural signal we believe to be meaningful. Setting the threshold higher risks including more CSF signal, while setting it lower risks excluding signal we are interested in.

Figure 1 shows a sagittal, coronal and axial slice with the estimated cranial dura overlaid on the -weighted MRI. Notice that this estimate is not continuous. For the purpose of tracer signal measurement for parameter estimation we primarily aim to identify regions which are highly likely to be dura. By imposing that the dura must be outside the CSF mask, and have a Look-Locker -time longer than fat and lower than CSF we are more likely to capture real dural tracer enrichment.

sec.title: Parameter estimation via reduced and explicit models
sec.p: In the following, we provide the first in vivo estimates of the transport properties of dural lymphatic clearance. We estimate tracer concentration at 4, 24, 48 and 72 hours following tracer injection in the cranial dura and in a thin layer of CSF < 2 mm from the dura. Parameters are estimated using a combination of explicit and geometrically reduced models. In the latter case, parameters are estimated using a Quasi Monte Carlo sampling approach and selected on the basis of the lowest mean-squared error compared to the data. We solve an advection-diffusion equation, modeling the transport in the dura mater and meningeal lymphatics, allowing for the estimation of a set of transport properties of dural lymphatic clearance. A set of subsidiary parameter estimates, providing input values for this model, are performed prior to the main parameter estimates. These models and corresponding estimates are summarized in the Supplementary Material.

sec.title: Model definition
sec.p: The transport of solutes within the cranial dura is governed by a coupled compartmental framework, which we employ to characterize the exchange between the subarachnoid space (SAS), the dural interstitial space, and the meningeal lymphatic system. In this model, we view the CSF in the SAS as the primary reservoir for solute influx; the dura acts as an intermediary compartment where solutes transition from the fluid-filled space into the active drainage network of the meningeal lymphatic vessels (mLVs).

sec.p: In this framework, the diffusion operator accounts for the stochastic, non-directed movement of solutes, while the advection operator describes the bulk, velocity-driven transport within the lymphatic vessels. The motivation for the remaining terms is rooted in the physiological interaction between the dura and its environment. Specifically, the term represents the trans-meningeal permeability, acting as the primary gateway for solutes crossing from the SAS into the dural interstitium based on the concentration gradient , where .

The interaction between the dural tissue and the lymphatic vessels is captured by the exchange coefficient β, which modulates the efficiency of solute transfer between the interstitium and the lymphatic drainage network. Crucially, we include the Starling filtration term to represent the pressure-driven bulk fluid flux across the dura-mLVs. This term is essential because it accounts for the fact that solute entry into the mLVs is not purely diffusive; rather, it is often coupled with the movement of fluid driven by hydrostatic and oncotic pressure gradients between the CSF and the dural space. Moreover, the partition coefficient is the ratio between the dura and the lymphatic porosities, and a better explanation of this coefficient is derived in Supplementary G.3.1. Finally, the clearance term acts as the model’s physiological “sink,” representing the downstream export of solutes into cervical lymphatic vessels, thereby completing the clearance pathway.

To ensure that these dynamics are driven by high-fidelity data, we estimate the SAS boundary concentration on a patch-by-patch basis as being less than 2 mm from the dura. In order to perform numerical time-stepping with higher time-resolution than the data measurements, we perform a non-linear least-squares fit of the raw MRI CSF tracer estimates, selecting the model with the minimum residual error between a Gamma distribution and a Double Exponential function. Across the 150 spatial patches, the Gamma distribution was selected 109 times (72.7%) and the Double Exponential 41 times (27.3%). These functional forms carry no mechanistic meaning; rather, they serve as purely empirical fitting tools. Selecting the fit with the lowest residual ensures that the continuous-time boundary conditions imposed on the ODE solver remain as faithful as possible to the raw in vivo MRI measurements, thereby minimizing input error prior to parameter estimation.

sec.p: From Eqs. Parameters were sampled within ranges informed by physiological data and established biomechanical properties of the dural and lymphatic tissues. Specifically, the partition coefficient ϕ and lymphatic volume fraction are constrained based on avaiable literature data (see Supplementary E). Permeability ( sampling limit is a wide range based on typical physiological values [32, 33], and diffusion () ranges was selected to cover typical values considering the possibility of both tortuosity and dispersion. Instead, the parameter was treated as unconstrained, with a non-informative (flat) prior distribution assigned to allow the data to determine its optimal value within the sampling range. Parameters are sampled using a Quasi Monte Carlo (QMC) Halton sampling method [34], which has faster convergence properties than purely stochastic Monte Carlo methods. sec.title: Implementation
sec.p: The cranial dura was spatially discretized utilizing a lumped-parameter network approach evaluated on a patch-by-patch basis. The dura and the nearby CSF space was partitioned into N=150 discrete regions (nodes). The spatial differential operators were translated into matrix form: The diffusion operator was approximated by constructing the graph Laplacian matrix, weighted by the Euclidean distances between the centers of mass of adjacent patches extracted from the MRI data. This formulation reduces the original continuous problem to a coupled system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), while retaining features of tracer transport in the brain. An intrathecal tracer will enter from below, first reaching the brainstem and cerebellar SAS, before moving into the rest of the brain. Reducing the geometry to patches retains the ability to solve the problem efficiently, thus enabling QMC estimates, while still keeping some key physiological structure.

The entire computational framework was developed in Python. Coupling rapid trans-dural exchanges (β) with slow interstitial diffusion renders the ODE system highly stiff. Time integration was therefore performed using the solve_ivp solver from the SciPy [41] library, employing implicit method (Radau). The differential operators were vectorized utilizing the scipy.sparse library to maximize computational efficiency during the Monte Carlo simulations. The solution space was explored by generating low-discrepancy quasi-random vectors via the scipy.stats.qmc module (Halton sequences). Subsequently, the simulations were ranked based on the IQR-weighted loss function. To ensure physiological robustness and filter out algorithmic noise, a Top Ensemble consisting exclusively of the best 200 fits was extracted.

sec.title: Three-dimensional model of the cranial dura
sec.p: We leverage the parameters computed using the methods outlined in Sect. 2.3 and apply them to a full 3D simulation of dura and meningeal lymphatic vessels on a realistic geometry of the cranial dura. We solve a double-porosity advection-diffusion model numerically in order to illustrate dural lymphatic clearance. First, we evaluate the ability of dura lymphatics to clear the CSF albumin content and, second, we perform data-integrated 72-hour simulations of gadobutrol in dural lymphatics and meningeal lymphatic vessels.

sec.p: Three-dimensional simulations are performed using a realistic representation of the cranial dura, shown in Fig. 3. sec.title: Clearance of albumin through dural lymphatics:
sec.p: We first design a simulation to investigate whether the lymphatic system can sufficiently manage protein clearance from the brain. Understanding this clearance is crucial, as impaired clearance and subsequent protein accumulation are hallmarks of many neurodegenerative diseases. Generally, CSF proteins are subject to various clearance mechanisms, including enzymatic degradation, transport across the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and lymphatic drainage. In our simulation, we specifically focus on albumin. While albumin is not a pathological protein associated with neurodegeneration, it is the most abundant protein in the CSF. Therefore, for simplicity, we use it as a representative proxy. Here, we hypothesize a model where all such protein clearance occurs via the dural lymphatic system, allowing us to assess whether the lymphatic network alone can account for total protein clearance [43]. For the Gonzo dataset, we have a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentration of protein of ≈ 0.73 g/L; typically, around 50 % of the protein content is albumin [44, 45], which leads to an albumin concentration of ≈ 0.36 g/L in the Gonzo dataset. sec.p: We design a simulation that models transport of the intrathecal gadobutrol tracer in the dura. In this case, is prescribed as a spatio-temporally varying concentration function using measured tracer concentration estimates at the dura-CSF interface. This simulation is therefore driven by actual measured data, taking advantage of the estimated geometry of the cranial dura.

sec.title: Tracer enrichment in the cranial dura
sec.p: Using the segmentation introduced in Sect. 2.2, illustrated in Fig. 1, we are able to quantify tracer in the dura. In Fig. 4 we plot the distribution of tracer concentration in the cranial dura and compare it to the thin layer of CSF within 1.5 mm of the dura. We plot the tracer distribution at each time-point using concentrations estimated with Look-Locker, the Mixed sequence and the Hybrid sequence [18]. The Hybrid sequence combines Look-Locker and Mixed sequences by using the Mixed sequence in CSF voxels where ms. We note that the CSF signal has a higher mean than the dura signal at all time-points and in all sequences. Note that the Mixed signal in the dura will be zero in the vast of voxels due to the design of the segmentation. Accordingly, the Look-Locker and Hybrid sequences will be essentially equivalent in the dura. We also note that the signal in the dura is subject to significant noise, the relative width of the concentration distribution in the dura is consistently wider than in the CSF. Using a right-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test and a right-tailed quantile test we find that the signal in the dura and CSF is significantly different from baseline at all time-points more than 4 hours after injection . At 4 hours, the signal is significantly different from baseline in the cerebellum-brainstem and anterior-inferior regions. Statistical tests are implemented in SciPy [41].

sec.p: Figure 5 still compares dura concentration with neighboring CSF, but we additionally split the brain into 5 regions to capture the spatial distribution of how tracer propagates in the SAS. Tracer will enter the brain from below, first reaching CSF spaces surrounding the brainstem and the cerebellum. Figure 5a shows that tracer concentration in the CSF in this region peaks at 4 hours post-injection, and decreases as the tracer rises in the brain. The tracer will then follow major cerebral arteries and propagate in the SAS first towards anterior and medial regions before reaching superior and posterior regions of the SAS. The posterior-inferior and anterior-inferior regions peak at 24 hours post-injection in both dura and CSF. Posterior and anterior superior regions peak at 48 hours. Figure 5b compares tracer concentration in the 5 regions in CSF and in the dura. While the CSF has a pronounced peak at 4 hours after injection in the cerebellum and brainstem, the concentration in the dura in the same region does not peak until 24 hours after injection. In other regions, the pattern of concentration in the dura is generally consistent with the CSF, although at a much lower value. In the dura, the most pronounced concentration peak appears in the posterior-inferior region 24 hours after injection, this is likely partially explained by signal leakage across the tentorium cerebelli. Using a right-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test and a right-tailed quantile test we find that at time-points more than 4 hours after injection, in all sequences (except Mixed in the dura), the post-injection signal is significantly different than baseline . At 4 hours after injection, the signal in the dura is not significant compared to baseline, while the CSF signal is only significant for the Look-Locker sequence. Statistical tests are implemented in SciPy [41].

sec.title: Parameter estimation in the cranial dura
sec.p: Table 2 shows estimates with median, interquartile range and 95th percentile confidence intervals for the partition coefficient ϕ, the CSF permeability , the lymphatic diffusion coefficient , the clearance rate to deep cervical lymphatic vessels and the lymphatic volume fraction . We also include relevant derived quantities like the Péclet number, the Biot number, the Advection time, the Diffusion time and the half-life of tracer absorption in the dura. Parameters were estimated from QMC simulation. The best-fit simulation achieved a minimum weighted Sum of Squared Residuals (SSR) of 0.055, with 582 data points (representing over 99% of the temporal series) successfully falling within the experimental interquartile range (IQR). To ensure the structural identifiability of the system, statistical inference was performed on a Top Ensemble of the 200 best-performing fits.

sec.title: Advection dominates diffusion in the meningeal lymphatic network
sec.p: To characterize the physical regime of tracer transport, we evaluated the lymphatic Péclet number (Pe), which quantifies the ratio between the rate of advection and the rate of pure diffusion. The (macroscopic) Péclet number was evaluated for the lymphatic phase with the estimated velocity and diffusion coefficient, using as a characteristic length scale the length of the whole brain (in z direction). Across the top performing samples, the model yielded a median Pe of 160.56 (IQR: 49.03–817.89). Because Pe ≫ 1, the results suggest that lymphatic clearance in the dura cannot be driven by diffusion alone. Instead, the system is fundamentally dominated by advective bulk flow, where the tracer is actively swept towards the basal drainage sites by interstitial fluid currents. Although compounding uncertainties from noisy macroscopic data result in a wide 95% confidence interval for this derived ratio Table 2, the lower bound strictly exceeds 1, confirming that tracer clearance is advection-dominated.

sec.title: Global lymphatic clearance is flow-limited
sec.p: To provide clinically relevant pharmacokinetic metrics, model rate constants were converted into half-lives (). The inlet half-life, representing tracer absorption from the CSF into the dura (), was estimated to be highly rapid at approximately 1.57 hours. In contrast, the outlet half-life, reflecting the final drainage from the basal lymphatic vessels into the deep cervical lymphatic vessels (), was nearly instantaneous ( minute). Because local uptake is fast and terminal outflow is instantaneous, the global macroscopic clearance of the brain is entirely limited by the transit time through the lymphatic network. Deriving the global half-life from the network’s advection time yields a median 15.83 hours (IQR: 9.41-26.95 h). This half-life is generally consistent with the typical 24-to-48 hour delayed clearance curves observed our clearance data, such as Fig. 5. We notice that without advection, the median half-time of diffusion alone is ≈ 2694 h (IQR: 782-13324 h).

sec.title: Evaluating the capacity of dural lymphatics in clearing albumin from CSF
sec.p: Using the albumin concentration obtained in Sect. 2.4.3, we estimate the half-life of albumin clearance from the brain by computing the outflux as in Eq. (18). Our results yield an estimated clearance half-life of h, which means a complete clearance of albumin over 1 day. Moreover, we have an outflux that is governed by the advective component. Figure 6 shows the simulation results. In particular, Fig. 6a represents the 3D simulation with a fixed constant concentration after reaching a steady state solution; Fig. 6b shows the outflux computed as in Eq. (18), decomposed in the advective and diffusive component, showing that the advective component is the most relevant one. Considering that [19] reports a baseline protein content of approximately 0.5 g/L in the subarachnoid space (SAS), these findings suggest that the intrinsic drainage capacity of the meningeal lymphatic network is more than sufficient to handle the baseline protein clearance volume of the whole brain. Consequently, the actual rate-limiting factor in the macroscopic clearance process appears to be the CSF flow delivering solutes through the SAS, rather than the drainage capacity of the mLVs themselves.

(c) Decomposition of the outlet flux into its advective and diffusive components, demonstrating that advection is the dominant mechanism for solute clearance compared to diffusion

sec.title: Data-integrated 72 hour simulations of intrathecal gadobutrol in the dura
sec.p: In Fig. 7, we compare the macroscopic tracer distribution derived from in vivo MRI with the OpenFOAM simulations over a 72-hour period. Both modalities exhibit a highly consistent temporal trend: a progressive wash-in phase that reaches peak concentration globally across the cortical surface at 24 hours, followed by a gradual wash-out phase at 48 and 72 hours. Spatially, the models demonstrate broad regional agreement, particularly during peak accumulation. However, a key distinction lies in the surface texture: while the OpenFOAM simulation yields smooth, idealized concentration gradients dictated by continuous fluid dynamics, the MRI reconstructions inevitably retain local heterogeneity. This variance reflects the inherent physiological noise and partial volume effects present when imaging the extremely thin layer of the cranial dura. Despite these modality-specific differences, the computational model successfully captures the primary bulk clearance dynamics observed in the patient data.

To mitigate noise, the MRI data was 3D median-filtered and thresholded to remove background signal and outliers ( > 95th percentile). Because the valid MRI data points are scattered, a distance-weighted K-Nearest neighbors (KNN) regression was used as a spatial interpolator. For a direct comparison, both MRI data and the OpenFOAM meshes were projected onto a continuous, shared dural reference mask using KNN. A uniform color scale is applied across all panels to highlight spatial gradients and clearance dynamics over time. (b) Spatial median concentration of the openFoam simulations and MRI data

sec.title: Tracer enrichment in the cranial dura
sec.p: A primary challenge in quantifying tracer dynamics is the thinness of the dura mater (typically 1–2 mm). Although the mm resolution of the Gonzo dataset (representing a single healthy subject), the dural layer spans only one to four voxels, resulting in data with significant noise. To ensure the validity of our measurements, our segmentation methodology deliberately prioritizes specificity over spatial continuity. By enforcing strict relaxation time thresholds (400 ms to 1705 ms) and rigid spatial boundaries relative to the CSF, we obtain a conservative estimate. This minimizes artifactual signal bleed-over from the subarachnoid space or subcutaneous fat, giving us high confidence that the isolated signal represents genuine macroscopic dural tracer enrichment. However, we notice that significant variation present in the concentration estimates in Figs. 4 and 5, particularly in the dura. We therefore additionally verify that the post-injection dura signal is significantly different than the pre-injection signal using non-parametric right-tailed tests. The signal in the dura and neighboring CSF is found to be significantly different from baseline in all sessions recorded more than 4 hours following injection. At 4 hours after injection, we do not find a significant difference compared to baseline in all regions. However, this is also to be expected as the tracer will not have reached all regions of the brain in such a short time-span after injection. Indeed, in Fig. 5, we find significant tracer enrichment in the cerebellum-brainstem region and anterior-posterior region at the early time-point, but not in other regions. These two regions with significant tracer concentration are also the regions that the tracer will reach first, and this is therefore to be expected.

Despite this robust approach, several limitations remain. First, the segmentation entirely excludes internal dural reflections, specifically the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. Because these structures are flanked by CSF, they are indistinguishable from the surrounding fluid at the current resolution. Second, our stringent thresholding inevitably discards some true dural tissue that falls outside these bounds. Finally, while our method successfully captures bulk tracer accumulation, the spatial resolution cannot directly resolve microscopic meningeal lymphatic vessels (mLVs). We must therefore rely on generalized cranial dural concentration as a proxy, which limits our ability to definitively isolate active lymphatic clearance from passive dural diffusion.

Although our segmentation pipeline employs conservative spatial boundaries and thresholding to isolate the dural signal, the inherent resolution limits of macroscopic in vivo MRI mean that some residual partial-volume contamination from the adjacent, high-signal CSF cannot be definitively ruled out. However, our signal exclusion criteria contribute to reducing the impact of such effects on the transport parameters we estimate.

sec.title: Parameter estimation in the cranial dura
sec.p: To our knowledge, this study represents one of the first attempts to derive macroscopic transport parameters for the human cranial dura and mLVs using in vivo inverse mathematical modeling. Because directly comparable inferred parameters are scarce in the current literature, a direct 1:1 comparison of macroscopic transport rates is challenging. Instead, we relied on existing quantitative experimental measurements to establish the physiological boundary constraints for our inverse problem and to find parameters value, ensuring our derived parameters remained firmly within realistic biological orders of magnitude.

sec.title: Advection dominates diffusion in the dura
sec.p: Our analysis suggests that in this subject the transport inside of meningeal lymphatic vessels is predominantly advection-dominated. These findings align with the literature [46], which demonstrate that cerebrospinal fluid and its solutes are cleared through the lymphatic system via bulk fluid re-uptake driven by distinct pressure gradients. Moreover, if we consider the velocities found in [47] of 2.2-2.7 mm/s, the diffusion coefficient in free water of gadobutrol /s, and a characteristics size of the vessel as in [2, 48, 49] of m, we obtain a miroscopic Péclet number of Taken together, this may explain our estimated higher diffusion (dispersion) coefficient for the lymphatic phase, and a macroscopic Péclet number ≫ 1.

sec.title: Global lymphatic clearance is flow-limited
sec.p: Our results indicate that macroscopic brain clearance is fundamentally flow-limited for the Gonzo dataset. With extremely rapid local CSF-to-dura absorption ( 1.5 h) and near-instantaneous terminal lymphatic drainage ( 5 min), global clearance is dictated by advective transit through the dural network (median advection 15.8 h). This matches our empirical 24-to-48 hour clearance curves and confirms that advection heavily dominates over diffusion (median diffusion h). However, a critical limitation is the low temporal resolution of the MRI data (4, 24, 48, and 72 hours). Due to the low temporal resolution, time lags on the order of hours (such as delays in peak concentration or temporal offsets between CSF and dural uptake) cannot be resolved. Moreover, we assumed that entirety of clearance from the dura is given by the mLVs. Therefore, our rapid local rate constants likely represent an upper theoretical bound for lymphatic clearance. While the overall flow-limited mechanism is robustly supported, specific clearance rates should be interpreted as upper estimates rather than exact physiological measurements.

sec.title: Evaluating the capacity of dural lymphatics in clearing albumin from CSF
sec.p: Our results suggest that in this subject meningeal lymphatic vessels (mLVs) possess the capacity to clear all CSF albumin within a single day. This robust clearance capability aligns with the classical homeostatic function of the peripheral lymphatic system. The estimated clearance mechanism may appear exceptionally strong, yielding a rapid half-life and maintaining a positive outflux even under extreme simulated concentrations. However, this should be interpreted as an upper-bound estimate of general mLV clearance. We deliberately modeled a scenario where mLVs are responsible for clearing all brain fluid to avoid parameter identifiability issues associated with parallel efflux routes (as detailed in Supplementary G) and to rigorously test the network’s absolute functional limits. By demonstrating that the mLVs can process loads vastly exceeding typical physiological needs within our subject-specific model, our findings indicate that the true rate-limiting factor in macroscopic brain clearance is likely not the intrinsic drainage capacity of the dural lymphatics themselves, but rather the upstream delivery of solutes via CSF flow through the subarachnoid space.

sec.title: Data-integrated 72 hour simulations of intrathecal gadobutrol in the dura
sec.p: Although the simulations effectively capture the tracer dynamics, the continuous nature of the mathematical models inherently contrasts with the limited temporal resolution of the MRI acquisitions. Consequently, caution must be exercised when interpreting early-phase clearance, ensuring a clear distinction between theoretical model predictions and actual empirical observations.

Furthermore, the parameter estimation for the 0D model was deliberately weighted by the interquartile range to account for the substantial physiological and methodological variability within the Gonzo dataset (see Fig. 4). Because this approach prioritizes the overall data distribution rather than strictly adhering to the median, the simulated trajectories do not perfectly align with the median empirical curve. This divergence is an intended outcome of the weighted fitting strategy; by consistently remaining within the bounds of the empirical IQR, the model successfully captures the underlying transport dynamics while robustly accounting for observed biological uncertainty.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, we investigated the complex hydrodynamics of cranial waste clearance by integrating patient-specific gMRI data, a novel anatomical segmentation of the dura, and a hierarchy of inverse mathematical and micro-mechanical models. By bridging the gap between clinical imaging and computational fluid dynamics, this approach allowed us to estimate previously inaccessible physiological parameters and subsequently inform a spatially distributed, double-porosity 3D computational model of the human dura.

While our parameter estimates and 3D simulations establish a robust baseline for understanding meningeal lymphatic clearance, we acknowledge that these estimations are subject to inherent computational uncertainties and further analysis is required. Crucially, to avoid parameter identifiability issues, we deliberately modeled a scenario where mLVs are responsible for clearing all brain fluid. Consequently, our conclusion that mLVs possess the theoretical capacity to clear all CSF albumin within a single day must be interpreted as an upper bound, as parallel efflux routes may be relevant. Future extensions of this work will focus on refining the system’s boundaries to create a fully integrated model of central nervous system waste clearance. Primarily, this involves achieving a tighter physical and mathematical coupling between our 3D dural model and the upstream CSF dynamics within the brain parenchyma [50]. Additionally, to improve the anatomical fidelity of the computational domain, future studies must employ a more realistic segmentation of the dura mater that explicitly incorporates complex internal reflections such as the falx and the tentorium cerebelli. Furthermore, future iterations should explicitly describe the downstream lymphatic transport network, extending the computational domain from the cranial dura all the way to the cervical lymph nodes, coupling our model with cervical collecting lymphatic and lymph node models [23, 38, 39, 51, 52].

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
